sections.description: This section introduces the case by detailing how the patient initially presented to the emergency department with neck swelling, the evolving clinical impressions, and the critical importance of thorough physical examination. It traces the clinical journey from initial suspicion of infection to consideration of angioedema, highlighting the key findings that ultimately redirected the diagnostic approach toward dermatomyositis.
subtopics: Patient demographics, medical history, and presenting symptoms (progressive neck swelling, proximal muscle weakness, myalgia)
Initial clinical impression: Ludwig's angina and deep neck space infection
ENT evaluation including CT neck findings and flexible nasendoscopy results
Transition to immunology consultation for suspected idiopathic angioedema
Critical physical examination findings: facial erythema, nailfold changes (periungual erythema, microhaemorrhages, avascular areas), thigh rash, and reduced hip flexor power
Atypical features for angioedema: absence of triggering factors, negative medication history, and absence of family history

sections.description: This section systematically explores the differential diagnosis for neck swelling, with particular emphasis on angioedema and its subtypes. It explains the clinical reasoning process used to narrow the differential and identifies the key features that made dermatomyositis a leading consideration despite its unusual presentation as pseudoangioedema.
subtopics: Comprehensive differential diagnosis: infectious causes (Ludwig's angina, deep neck space infections, cellulitis), angioedema, inflammatory myopathies, superior vena cava syndrome, orofacial granulomatosis, and drug reactions
Angioedema classification: histaminergic (allergic), bradykinin-mediated (hereditary and acquired), and non-mediated causes
Workup for angioedema: complement levels (C3, C4), C1 esterase function and quantification
Why this presentation was atypical for angioedema: clinical profile inconsistency with acquired or hereditary forms
Red flags prompting broader investigation: elevated CRP, presence of skin/nail changes, proximal muscle weakness
The pivotal role of creatine kinase testing in redirecting the diagnostic approach

sections.description: This section details the comprehensive diagnostic workup that confirmed dermatomyositis, including serological testing, imaging modalities, and tissue biopsy. It explains how each investigation contributed to establishing the diagnosis and assessing disease extent, culminating in the definitive diagnosis of anti-SAE1 antibody-positive dermatomyositis.
subtopics: Laboratory investigations: significantly elevated creatine kinase (16,184 U/L), elevated transaminases (ALT, AST), LDH elevation, and their interpretation in muscle disease
Serological findings: positive ANA (1:1280, speckled pattern), myositis antibody panel results with strongly positive anti-SAE1 antibodies
Imaging studies: CT neck findings, CT chest (pulmonary nodules, peribronchial consolidation), MRI thighs showing active myositis, FDG-PET scan demonstrating diffuse muscle inflammation
Muscle biopsy pathology: perifascicular distribution of necrotic and regenerative myofibers, perimysial inflammation, C5b-9 deposition in perifascicular endomysial capillaries
Functional assessments: video fluoroscopic swallow study showing severe pharyngeal dysphagia, pulmonary function tests showing extrathoracic restrictive pattern
Malignancy screening: CT abdomen, PET scan, tumor markers, and planned endoscopic evaluation

sections.description: This section provides the essential pathophysiological and clinical background on dermatomyositis necessary to understand this case. It covers the disease mechanisms, the significance of anti-SAE1 antibodies, and explains the uncommon phenomenon of pseudoangioedema in dermatomyositis, providing context for why this presentation was diagnostically challenging.
subtopics: Overview of dermatomyositis: definition, epidemiology (incidence, bimodal distribution), and clinical features
Classic cutaneous manifestations: Gottron's papules, heliotrope eruption, shawl sign, V-neck sign, periungual telangiectasias
Anti-SAE1 antibodies: target antigen (SUMO activating enzyme), role in 'sumoylation', and clinical phenotype associations
Clinical spectrum of SAE1-positive dermatomyositis: cutaneous features, dysphagia (46%), interstitial lung disease (43%), malignancy risk (18%)

Pseudoangioedema in dermatomyositis: mechanism (subcutaneous edema from muscle inflammation vs histaminergic/bradykinin-mediated angioedema), prevalence (6.61% in one cohort), and clinical implications
Malignancy risk stratification using IMACS guidelines: high-risk factors (dermatomyositis, dysphagia), intermediate-risk factors (SAE1 antibody, male sex)

sections.description: This section explains the therapeutic approach for this patient, detailing the rationale for medication selection and the clinical reasoning behind specific treatment choices. It covers acute management, long-term immunosuppression strategy, supportive care, and important considerations such as medication contraindications and infection prophylaxis.
subtopics: Acute management: IV methylprednisolone (1000 mg daily for 3 days) and indications for aggressive initial immunosuppression
Long-term immunosuppression: prednisone tapering regimen, mycophenolate mofetil dosing and rationale for selection
Adjunctive therapies: IVIG loading and maintenance regimen, rituximab dosing schedule
Medications avoided and reasons: methotrexate (interstitial lung disease concern), azathioprine and tacrolimus (mycophenolate well-tolerated)
Infection prophylaxis: initial sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, switch to nebulized pentamidine due to hemolytic anemia
Supportive care: nasogastric tube feeding for dysphagia, rehabilitation considerations
Pre-treatment screening: hepatitis B/C, HIV, VZV, CMV, and tuberculosis status

sections.section_title: Clinical Outcome, Follow-up, and Key Lessons
sections.description: This section describes the patient's clinical course following treatment, including his hospital stay, recovery trajectory, and ongoing management. It summarizes the key clinical lessons from this case that are applicable to future clinical practice, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis and recognizing atypical presentations of connective tissue diseases.
subtopics: Hospital course: 21-day inpatient stay, persistence of dysphagia requiring nasogastric tube at discharge
Recovery timeline: normalization of CK by 3 weeks, resolution of cervical swelling by 3 months, complete dysphagia resolution by 7 months
Ongoing management: mycophenolate tapering plan, continued IVIG, malignancy surveillance strategy
Malignancy surveillance: clinical monitoring, serial CT chest imaging, planned gastroscopy and colonoscopy
Clinical pearls: importance of CK testing in unexplained neck swelling, thorough skin and nail examination, recognizing pseudoangioedema
Key diagnostic lesson: dermatomyositis should be considered in differential diagnosis of unexplained neck swelling, especially when atypical for angioedema
Multidisciplinary approach: role of emergency medicine, ENT, immunology, and rheumatology in accurate diagnosis
